title: Problem Solving and Ego Development
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart extends Mary Kennedy's framing of teaching as a set of persistent problems upward into school leadership, treating problem solving as a golden thread running from the classroom through the school to system level. Building on Barker and Rees, he offers his own list of six persistent problems of school leadership, from organising the curriculum and influencing student culture to allocating resources and activating the community, and then does the more useful work of naming the barrier attached to each. Leaders provide strategic direction to staff with varying beliefs about education, influence student culture where peer dynamics may outweigh adult intentions, and allocate resources where funding rarely meets the needs of every child. The pivot in the piece is Kennedy's fifth challenge, accommodating personal needs, which for leaders becomes the persistent problem of the self. Hart argues that a leader's capacity to solve every external problem is bounded by their ability to make sense of complexity, and he brings in Neil Gilbride's work on adult ego development, where a leader's developmental stage determines what they can notice, describe, reflect on and do. He invites readers to self-diagnose against Gilbride's stages, then draws the practical implication that leadership preferences show up in what leaders repeatedly talk about, whether displays, marking or tucked-in shirts. He also flags the attribution trap, that a leader who presided over improvement will naturally credit the strategies they themselves advocated. The conclusion is modest and honest, that reflecting on our own needs is clearly worth doing while how to develop one's ego remains an open question.
points: The structural move is treating leadership as a fixed set of persistent problems that manifest differently by context rather than a list of competencies.
Hart's most useful addition is pairing each leadership problem with its characteristic barrier, such as peer dynamics overpowering adult intentions in student culture.
The self is reframed as a persistent problem in its own right, on the argument that a leader's sense-making capacity bounds every other solution they can reach.
Gilbride's adult ego development stages are used as a diagnostic, with the claim that developmental stage governs what a leader is even able to notice and describe.
He names a specific self-deception risk: leaders who oversaw improvement will assign cause to the strategies they happened to champion.
quotes: Previously I have argued that problem solving is a golden thread from what teachers do each day in their classrooms, through to what leaders do across their school and finally to what system leaders do across multiple schools.
Leaders influence student culture where peer dynamics might have a stronger effect on collective behaviour than the good intentions of the adults.
Leaders provide strategic direction that communicates purpose to a staffing body that may have varying beliefs about education, school life and teaching.

The extent to which a school leader can make sense of the complexity of school leadership and go about the difficult work of improving schools relies on their beliefs and assumptions; plus leaders will have needs and preferences like anyone else to feel comfortable in their leadership behaviours and decisions.
Neil Gilbride writes and talks about adult ego development (AED); that the stage of development in a leader ‘affects what an individual is aware of and can describe, reflect upon and do’.

It is fairly obvious that wherever a leader sits within these stages of development will mean that they have certain needs and preferences that will significantly affect how they might go about solving all the other external persistent problems of school leadership.

We might show what we prefer through what we pay attention to, such as the leader who talks most often about the displays around the school or marking or shirts needing to be tucked in or countless other aspects of school life.

Some of these things might be inextricably linked with how we think schools get better. If we have presided over school improvement, it is natural to assign cause to the effect, particularly in the strategies or approaches that we have advocated and implemented.

If it is possible to reflect on our own needs as leaders, we ought to do it because those needs that our decisions are unavoidably based around might affect our school communities positively or negatively.
